title: Why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:33–41)
hook: he cries the first line of Psalm 22, and a Roman soldier says: truly the Son of God; the women watch

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crown of thorns and a crowd of mockers, Golgotha, and your line was he saved others.

Some of the hardest words anyone says are said at a hospital bedside, at 3am, when no answer comes. Why? Where are you? Mark doesn't soften what happens next. At the sixth hour, around noon, darkness covers the whole land until the ninth hour, about three in the afternoon. Then Jesus cries out with a loud voice. Mark gives the words in Aramaic, then translates them. They are the only words from the cross that Mark records.
screen: `DARKNESS AT NOON.` → `THE NINTH HOUR.` → `A LOUD CRY.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those words weren't new: they're the opening line of Psalm 22. The psalm starts in anguish: surrounded, mocked, bones out of joint, enemies dividing his garments. It ends in trust, the psalmist praising God in the great congregation. Christians read the cry in different ways, and the readings sit together. Some hear real abandonment, the Son going all the way down into the silence people feel when God seems gone. Others suggest that naming a psalm's first line can call up the whole psalm, so he may be praying all of Psalm 22, ending included. Some hold both. Either way, it matters that the prayer of the dying Jesus is a question. Some bystanders say: he's calling Elijah! One runs to give him sour wine on a sponge. Then Jesus gives a loud cry and breathes his last. At that moment, Mark says, the curtain of the temple is torn in two, from top to bottom. And the Roman centurion standing facing him, the soldier in charge of the execution, says: "Truly this man was the Son of God." Mark's gospel, in the King James text, opens by calling Jesus the Son of God. Now, at the cross, the one who says it out loud is not a disciple but a Roman soldier. And watching from a distance: the women. Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome, and many others who had followed him from Galilee. The disciples had fled. The women stayed.
screen: `ELOI, ELOI, LAMA SABACHTHANI?` · `THE FIRST LINE OF PSALM 22.` · `THE CURTAIN TORN, TOP TO BOTTOM.` · `THE WOMEN WATCHED.` · then, large: `TRULY THIS MAN WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: If you can, open Psalm 22 in any Bible and read it slowly, all the way through, noticing where it's darkest and where it turns. If you can't, sit with its first line, my God, my God, why, and think of someone asking that question right now. You don't need an answer for them; the women didn't have one either, they just stayed.
Eloi, Aramaic for my God, the first word of Jesus's cry from the cross. The opening line of Psalm 22, cried aloud in anguish and trust.
Your line: the women stayed. When words run out, staying can still say something. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some churches hold a service on Good Friday afternoon, around the ninth hour, and some pray Psalm 22 or meditate on the last words of Jesus from all four Gospels.

chat.says: Why would Jesus cry 'My God, why have you forsaken me?' on the cross?
options: It's Psalm 22's first line; some hear real abandonment, some the psalm's trust.
He was calling out for the prophet Elijah to come down and save him.
He was saying a curse aloud, so the crowd would leave him alone.
chat.meaning: Eloi, Eloi opens Psalm 22, which moves from anguish to trust. Christians hear real abandonment, the whole psalm, or both.

lama sabachthani.meaning: Aramaic: why have you forsaken me?

Psalm 22.meaning: a psalm that starts in anguish and ends in trust

centurion.meaning: the Roman officer in charge of the execution

Mary Magdalene.meaning: a follower from Galilee who stayed and watched

notes: 'The only saying from the cross in Mark': Mark 15:34 is the only recorded words; 15:37 is a wordless loud cry. Confirm.
Citing a psalm by its first line to call up the whole psalm: a common scholarly suggestion, presented as one reading among others.
Hebrew of Psalm 22:2 (22:1 in English numbering) given in the original game; confirm pointing and transliteration.
The centurion's words can also be read 'a son of God' (no article); the script uses the KJV.
